subtopic: Scientific Revolutions, Human Flourishing, & Global Issues

items.definition: The astronomical model proposed by Nicolaus Copernicus stating that the Sun, rather than the Earth, is at the center of the solar system.
items.rationalization: Copernicus displaced Ptolemy's ancient geocentric model, sparking the Scientific Revolution and transforming humanity's cosmic worldview.

mnemonic.title: Copernicus Heliocentrism
items: S - Shifted Earth away from center

items.tosCompetency: Analyze scientific revolutions and paradigm shifts

items.definition: Charles Darwin's mechanism for biological evolution stating that organisms with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully.
items.rationalization: Published in 'On the Origin of Species' (1859); challenged creationist doctrines by explaining the diversity of life through descent with modification.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze scientific revolutions and paradigm shifts

items.definition: The revolutionary psychological paradigm asserting that human behavior and personality are largely governed by unconscious desires, repressed memories, and the conflict between Id, Ego, and Superego.
items.rationalization: Freud revolutionized modern thought by proving that rational human consciousness is merely the tip of the mental iceberg, fundamentally reshaping society and medicine.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze scientific revolutions and paradigm shifts

items.definition: The Italian polymath regarded as the 'Father of Modern Observational Astronomy' and 'Father of Modern Physics' who used the telescope to discover Jupiter's moons and lunar craters.
items.rationalization: Galileo provided empirical observational proof for Copernicus's heliocentrism, enduring trial and house arrest by the Roman Inquisition for his findings.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze scientific revolutions and paradigm shifts

items.definition: Heidegger's philosophical concept in 'The Question Concerning Technology' describing how modern technology treats nature as a mere 'standing-reserve' (Bestand) to be exploited.
items.rationalization: Heidegger warned that technology is not a neutral tool; its essence is a way of revealing (Enframing) that blinds humanity to poetic and authentic existence.

mnemonic.title: Heidegger's Gestell
mnemonic.phrase: Gestell = Enframing Nature as Standing Reserve

items.tosCompetency: Examine philosophical perspectives on human flourishing and technology

items.definition: The Greek concept articulated by Aristotle meaning 'human flourishing', 'living well', and true happiness attained through the practice of virtue (arete).
items.rationalization: In STS, eudaimonia is the benchmark for whether scientific progress and technological innovations truly elevate human life or degrade human values.
items.tosCompetency: Examine philosophical perspectives on human flourishing and technology

items.definition: The renowned Filipino pediatrician and National Scientist who invented the bamboo incubator and founded the Children's Medical Center in the Philippines.
items.rationalization: She was the first Asian and first woman admitted to Harvard Medical School; her bamboo incubator provided lifesaving care in rural Philippine clinics lacking electricity.
items.tosCompetency: Identify Filipino scientists and their national contributions

items.definition: The Filipino National Scientist who invented a groundbreaking method to induce prolific flowering in mango trees year-round using potassium nitrate ($KNO_3$).
items.rationalization: His invention revolutionized the Philippine fruit industry, turning mangoes into one of the country's leading agricultural exports.

mnemonic.title: Barba Mango Clue
mnemonic.phrase: Barba = Blooms Mangoes with Potassium Nitrate

items.tosCompetency: Identify Filipino scientists and their national contributions

items.definition: The Filipino marine biologist and National Scientist recognized for inventing artificial coral reefs and establishing community-managed marine protected areas in the Philippines.
items.rationalization: His pioneering conservation work at Apo Island and across the Visayas rehabilitated devastated reef ecosystems and restored fish biomass.
items.tosCompetency: Identify Filipino scientists and their national contributions

items.definition: The Filipino inventor who held the official patent for the Sing-Along System (SAS), widely recognized as the Karaoke machine.
items.rationalization: Del Rosario won landmark legal battles in the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) and Philippine courts defending his 1970s patent against Japanese claimants.

mnemonic.title: Karaoke Inventor
mnemonic.phrase: Del Rosario Rocks the Karaoke Sing-Along

items.tosCompetency: Identify Filipino scientists and their national contributions

items.definition: The Filipino National Scientist and engineer who invented the two-way television-telephone (videophone) in 1955, as well as an aircraft engine fueled by pure alcohol.
items.rationalization: His videophone was decades ahead of modern video calling technology (Zoom, FaceTime); he holds 30 patents for innovative physical devices.
items.tosCompetency: Identify Filipino scientists and their national contributions

items.definition: A genetically modified crop engineered with a gene from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis producing an endotoxin that protects against the Asian corn borer pest.
items.rationalization: Bt corn drastically reduces the need for synthetic chemical insecticides, demonstrating the direct agricultural application of recombinant DNA technology.
items.tosCompetency: Evaluate applications and ethics of genetic engineering and biotechnology

items.definition: A genetically modified variety of Oryza sativa biosynthesized to produce beta-carotene (provitamin A) in the edible endosperm of the rice grain.
items.rationalization: Developed to alleviate Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) in developing countries, which causes childhood blindness, immune weakness, and infant mortality.

mnemonic.title: Golden Rice Benefit
mnemonic.phrase: Gold for Eyes: Beta-Carotene Vitamin A

items.tosCompetency: Evaluate applications and ethics of genetic engineering and biotechnology

items.definition: A revolutionary gene-editing technology adapted from a bacterial immune system that acts as molecular scissors to cut and modify DNA sequences with extreme precision.
items.rationalization: Developed by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020); enables targeted gene therapies, crop improvements, and disease eradication.
items.tosCompetency: Evaluate applications and ethics of genetic engineering and biotechnology

items.definition: An international agreement governing the movements of living modified organisms (LMOs) resulting from modern biotechnology from one country to another.
items.rationalization: Ensures the safe transfer, handling, and use of LMOs to protect global biodiversity and human health under the Convention on Biological Diversity.
items.tosCompetency: Evaluate applications and ethics of genetic engineering and biotechnology

items.definition: The natural process by which atmospheric gases trap infrared radiation from the Earth's surface, warming the planet to temperatures capable of sustaining life.
items.rationalization: Without the greenhouse effect, Earth would be a frozen wasteland (~ -18°C). The crisis is the ENHANCED greenhouse effect driven by human fossil fuel emissions.

mnemonic.title: Greenhouse Gases
mnemonic.phrase: Carbon, Methane, Water Vapor, Nitrous Oxide

items.tosCompetency: Analyze climate change, global warming, and environmental crises

items.definition: A landmark legally binding international treaty aimed at limiting global warming to well below 2°C, preferably to 1.5°C, compared to pre-industrial levels.
items.rationalization: Adopted by 196 nations at COP21 in Paris; mandates nationally determined contributions (NDCs) to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze climate change, global warming, and environmental crises

items.definition: A highly successful international environmental treaty designed to phase out the production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances, primarily chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
items.rationalization: Allowed the Antarctic stratospheric ozone layer to begin healing; recognized as one of the most effective international environmental accords in history.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze climate change, global warming, and environmental crises

items.term: RA 9003: Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000
items.definition: The Philippine law providing an ecological solid waste management program, mandating waste segregation at source, recycling, and the closure of open dumpsites.
items.rationalization: Mandates local government units (LGUs) to establish Materials Recovery Facilities (MRFs) and enforce segregation into biodegradable, recyclable, residual, and special wastes.
items.tosCompetency: Examine Philippine environmental laws and sustainable development policies

items.term: RA 8749: Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999
items.definition: The comprehensive national air pollution management policy designed to achieve and maintain clean air for all Filipinos, banning medical waste incineration.
items.rationalization: Imposes strict vehicle emission testing, regulates industrial factory emissions, and penalizes heavy polluters to safeguard public respiratory health.

mnemonic.title: RA 8749 Clue
items: B - Ban on municipal waste incineration

items.tosCompetency: Examine Philippine environmental laws and sustainable development policies

items.term: RA 9275: Philippine Clean Water Act of 2004
items.definition: The law aimed at protecting the country's water bodies from land-based pollution sources including domestic sewage, industrial wastewater, and agricultural runoff.
items.rationalization: Establishes Water Quality Management Areas (WQMAs) and requires discharge permits for businesses disposing effluents into river systems.
items.tosCompetency: Examine Philippine environmental laws and sustainable development policies

items.definition: The science, engineering, and technology conducted at the nanoscale, specifically measuring between 1 and 100 nanometers.
items.rationalization: At this scale, quantum mechanical effects dominate, giving materials dramatically altered electrical, thermal, chemical, and optical properties.
items.tosCompetency: Examine emerging technologies and nanoscale science

items.definition: The Nobel laureate physicist who introduced the foundational vision of nanotechnology in his 1959 lecture 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom'.
items.rationalization: Feynman envisioned manipulating individual atoms and molecules directly, foreseeing micro-machines, synthesized molecular computers, and atomic-scale engineering.

mnemonic.title: Feynman Nanotech
mnemonic.phrase: Plenty of Room at the Bottom

items.tosCompetency: Examine emerging technologies and nanoscale science

items.definition: A single two-dimensional layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal honeycomb lattice, renowned as the thinnest, strongest, and most conductive material known.
items.rationalization: Discovered by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov (Nobel Prize in Physics 2010); 200 times stronger than steel, transparent, and an extraordinary conductor of electricity.
items.tosCompetency: Examine emerging technologies and nanoscale science

items.definition: The invention by Johannes Gutenberg utilizing movable metal type and oil-based ink that triggered the information explosion in Renaissance Europe.
items.rationalization: Democratized knowledge by drastically reducing book production costs, sparking the Protestant Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and widespread public literacy.
items.tosCompetency: Trace the evolution of the Information Age and communication revolutions

items.definition: The English mathematician and cryptanalyst hailed as the 'Father of Theoretical Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence' who broke the Nazi Enigma code.
items.rationalization: Conceptualized the 'Turing Machine' and proposed the 'Turing Test' to assess whether a machine possesses intelligent behavior indistinguishable from a human.
items.tosCompetency: Trace the evolution of the Information Age and communication revolutions

items.definition: The British computer scientist who invented the World Wide Web (WWW) in 1989 at CERN, developing HTML, HTTP, and URLs.
items.rationalization: Crucially, he made the underlying code royalty-free and open to the public, unleashing the global digital interconnectedness of the internet.
items.tosCompetency: Trace the evolution of the Information Age and communication revolutions

items.definition: The empirical observation by Gordon Moore stating that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles roughly every two years while the cost of computers is halved.
items.rationalization: Drove the exponential explosion of computing power, miniaturization of consumer electronics, and rapid obsolescence of digital technology for over five decades.
items.tosCompetency: Trace the evolution of the Information Age and communication revolutions

items.definition: The Philippine law that protects individual personal data in information and communications systems in both the government and private sectors.
items.rationalization: Created the National Privacy Commission (NPC); mandates compliance with transparency, legitimate purpose, and proportionality when handling personal information.

mnemonic.title: RA 10173 Privacy
items: P - Privacy rights of data subjects

items.tosCompetency: Analyze cyber-ethics, privacy laws, and social media impacts

items.definition: The Philippine law penalizing offenses committed against and by means of computer systems, such as illegal access, data interference, cybersex, child pornography, and online libel.
items.rationalization: Provides legal remedies against hacking, identity theft, ATM fraud, and digital defamation in cyberspace.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze cyber-ethics, privacy laws, and social media impacts

items.definition: A renewable clean energy harnessed from the internal heat of the Earth, in which the Philippines is historically one of the world's top producers.
items.rationalization: Located along the Pacific Ring of Fire, major plants in Leyte, MakBan (Laguna/Batangas), and Tiwi (Albay) provide substantial clean baseload electricity.

mnemonic.title: Geothermal Ring
mnemonic.phrase: Earth Heat from Ring of Fire

items.tosCompetency: Evaluate alternative and renewable energy systems in the Philippines

items.definition: The local, traditional, and experiential knowledge, skills, and philosophies developed by indigenous communities across generations.
items.rationalization: Includes natural crop cycling, ethnobotanical herbal cures (lagundi, ampalaya), climate indicators from animal behavior, and sustainable water management.
items.tosCompetency: Value indigenous knowledge systems and practices alongside modern science

items.definition: The concept articulated in 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962) where an established scientific framework collapses under anomalies and is replaced by a fundamentally new paradigm.
items.rationalization: Scientific progress is not purely linear accumulation; it proceeds through normal science, crisis, and revolutionary paradigm shifts (e.g., Newtonian physics to Einstein's relativity).
items.tosCompetency: Analyze scientific revolutions and paradigm shifts

items.definition: The four core ethical principles governing biomedical research and healthcare: Autonomy, Non-maleficence, Beneficence, and Justice.
items.rationalization: Autonomy respects patient self-determination; Non-maleficence means 'do no harm'; Beneficence promotes positive good; Justice demands fair allocation of medical resources.

mnemonic.title: Four Bioethics Pillars
mnemonic.phrase: ANBJ: Autonomy, No harm, Beneficence, Justice

items.tosCompetency: Apply bioethical principles to biomedical issues and clinical research

items.definition: The simulation of human intelligence processes by computer systems, encompassing machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and autonomous reasoning.
items.rationalization: AI presents transformative benefits in healthcare diagnostics and climate modeling, alongside ethical dilemmas regarding algorithmic bias, job displacement, and autonomous weapons.
items.tosCompetency: Assess ethical dilemmas in artificial intelligence and automation

items.definition: Systematic and repeatable errors in computer software systems that create unfair outcomes, such as privileging one demographic category over another.
items.rationalization: Arises when training datasets reflect historic human prejudices or underrepresent marginalized groups (e.g., facial recognition errors on dark-skinned women).
items.tosCompetency: Assess ethical dilemmas in artificial intelligence and automation

items.definition: The ongoing decrease in the pH of the Earth's oceans caused by the uptake of anthropogenic carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) from the atmosphere.
items.rationalization: Absorbed $CO_2$ forms carbonic acid ($H_2CO_3$), depleting carbonate ions needed by corals, clams, and marine calcifiers to build skeletons and shells.

mnemonic.title: Acidifying Seas
mnemonic.phrase: $CO_2$ Plus Ocean Water Equals Carbonic Acid

items.tosCompetency: Analyze climate change, global warming, and environmental crises

items.definition: A metric that measures the total biologically productive land and water area required to produce the resources an individual or population consumes and absorb their waste.
items.rationalization: When humanity's ecological footprint exceeds the planet's biocapacity, Earth enters ecological overshoot, depleting natural capital for future generations.
items.tosCompetency: Examine sustainability metrics and ecological footprints

items.definition: Plastic fragments less than 5 millimeters in length resulting from commercial product breakdown and microbeads, contaminating marine ecosystems and food chains.
items.rationalization: Microplastics bioaccumulate in seafood, adsorbing toxic persistent organic pollutants (POPs) that ultimately reach human digestive and circulatory systems.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze environmental toxins and global pollution impacts

items.definition: The principle asserting that when an activity threatens grave or irreversible environmental or human harm, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used to postpone preventive measures.
items.rationalization: Found in Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration on Environment and Development; shifts the burden of proof to proponents of potentially hazardous technologies.
items.tosCompetency: Apply environmental ethics and international sustainability principles

items.definition: An economic model designed to minimize waste and maximize resource efficiency by keeping products and materials in use through sharing, leasing, reuse, repair, and recycling.
items.rationalization: Replaces the traditional linear economy ('take-make-dispose') with closed loops, regenerating natural systems and decoupling growth from resource exhaustion.
items.tosCompetency: Examine sustainability metrics and ecological footprints

items.definition: An advanced meteorological radar that uses the Doppler effect to measure precipitation intensity, cloud velocity, and storm rotation in real time.
items.rationalization: Allowed PAGASA to issue localized rainfall warnings and track typhoon landfall paths with pinpoint accuracy, saving thousands of lives during disasters.

mnemonic.title: Doppler Advantage
mnemonic.phrase: Tracks Storm Speed and Rain Intensity

items.tosCompetency: Identify Filipino scientists and technological disaster mitigation systems

items.definition: The first Philippine microsatellite launched into orbit in 2016, built by Filipino engineers from DOST and UP in collaboration with Japanese universities.
items.rationalization: Provided high-resolution multispectral earth observation for agricultural monitoring, forestry protection, disaster risk assessment, and coastal mapping.
items.tosCompetency: Identify Philippine space agency breakthroughs and satellite programs

items.definition: The government agency created by the Philippine Space Act of 2019 to manage the national space program, satellite data, and space infrastructure.
items.rationalization: Established to bolster national security, hazard management, climate forecasting, and commercial aerospace development in the country.
items.tosCompetency: Identify Philippine space agency breakthroughs and satellite programs

items.definition: Langdon Winner's concept describing how humans sleepwalk through life willingly accepting and adopting new technologies without reflecting on their profound social and moral transformations.
items.rationalization: Critiques human complacency where society unquestioningly adopts smartphones or algorithms without considering privacy loss or cognitive degradation.
items.tosCompetency: Examine philosophical perspectives on human flourishing and technology

items.definition: An experimental medical technique that treats or prevents genetic diseases by inserting, altering, or replacing faulty genes inside an individual's cells.
items.rationalization: Distinguishes between Somatic gene therapy (modifies non-reproductive cells; changes are not inherited) and Germline gene therapy (modifies sperm/egg; inheritable and heavily regulated).

mnemonic.title: Gene Therapy Types
mnemonic.phrase: Somatic Stays with Patient; Germline Passes to Children

items.tosCompetency: Evaluate applications and ethics of genetic engineering and biotechnology

items.definition: The use of undifferentiated stem cells to generate healthy cells that replace diseased, damaged, or aging tissues in the body.
items.rationalization: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (can form any tissue) but involve ethical controversies; induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer adult somatic alternatives.

mnemonic.title: Stem Cell Potential
mnemonic.phrase: Blank Cells that Become Any Tissue

items.tosCompetency: Evaluate applications and ethics of genetic engineering and biotechnology

items.definition: The systematic, empirical procedure of acquiring knowledge through observation, question formulation, hypothesis testing, controlled experimentation, and conclusion verification.
items.rationalization: Pioneered by Francis Bacon (Inductive method) and Rene Descartes (Deductive reasoning); forms the bedrock of replicable empirical inquiry.

mnemonic.title: Steps of Scientific Method
mnemonic.phrase: O-P-H-E-C: Observation, Problem, Hypothesis, Experiment, Conclusion

items.tosCompetency: Apply the steps and logic of the scientific method

items.definition: The evaluation of scientific, academic, or research work by qualified experts in the same field before publication in scholarly journals.
items.rationalization: Acts as the primary quality-control mechanism of modern science, weeding out flawed methodology, invalid data, fabrication, and unwarranted conclusions.
items.tosCompetency: Examine scholarly verification and peer-review rigor in science

items.definition: Aristotle and Heidegger's classical distinction where Techne is human skill, craft, and art, while Poiesis is poetic bringing-forth or uncovering truth.
items.rationalization: Ancient craft was a harmonious bringing-forth (Poiesis) of nature's beauty, whereas modern technology is an aggressive extracting and stockpiling (Gestell).
items.tosCompetency: Examine philosophical perspectives on human flourishing and technology
